title: MISP
summary: MISP is an open-source threat intelligence platform designed for storing, correlating, sharing and consuming structured indicators together with the context that makes them usable. Its central data structure is the event, a container that groups attributes describing an incident, campaign or sighting. Attributes are typed key-value pairs covering network indicators, file hashes and names, email artefacts, registry keys, financial data and free text, and they carry a category, a distribution setting and optional identifiers used for correlation. Objects extend attributes into structured bundles, so a file object can carry hashes, size and filename together instead of as loose rows. Taxonomies provide controlled vocabularies for classifying events, while galaxies attach knowledge such as ATT&CK techniques and threat actor clusters, which is what lets an organisation pivot from raw indicators to behavioural intelligence. Correlation is a core feature: when a newly ingested attribute matches an existing one, MISP links the events, surfacing relationships that a flat feed would hide. Sharing is governed by distribution levels, sharing groups and synchronisation with partner servers, and feeds can be pulled from external sources at configurable intervals. Warning lists are the practical counterweight to that automation, flagging values such as common public resolvers, popular domains and shared hosting ranges that are almost always benign. Effective MISP use depends on hygiene rather than features: consistent tagging, honest confidence and distribution choices, curated feeds, and periodic review of stale events. Because instances frequently exchange data with partners and public feeds, every ingested attribute should be treated as untrusted input, and correlation output should never drive automatic blocking without a validation step.
objectives: You will be able to model an incident as a MISP event with typed attributes and objects rather than loose indicators.
You will be able to apply taxonomies and galaxies so an event carries classification and technique context.
You will be able to configure distribution levels and sharing groups so intelligence reaches only intended partners.
You will be able to explain how correlation and warning lists change what an analyst sees and what gets blocked.
You will be able to evaluate and curate external feeds and retire stale events from an instance.
You will be able to assess the exposure created by publishing an event and choose the correct sharing setting.
